s: Part one.
Agentic loops.
This is task statement one point one: design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution.
By the end of this part, you'll know how to read why the model stopped, how to handle each reason, and why the decision to stop belongs to your code, not the model.
Start with the difference between asking and sending.
Ask a friend a question, and you get one answer.
Then it's over.
Now send that friend to the shops with a list.
Something different happens.
They find an item out of stock, and pick a substitute.
They see a long queue, and try another till.
You scripted none of that.
They made a series of small decisions on the way to the goal.
That's the difference between a single call to a model and an agent.
The same ability to produce an answer, wrapped in a loop.
The model picks an action.
Your code carries it out.
The result goes back in.
The loop runs again.
Here's the part architects get wrong.
A real friend gets tired and comes home.
An agent doesn't.
It has no clock.
No fatigue.
And no view of your bank balance.
It will keep taking reasonable-looking next steps until something outside it says stop.
So who decides when to stop?
You do.
The decision to stop belongs to you.
In plain terms, every time the model stops producing text, it tells you why.
It finished its thought.
It hit a length limit.
It's waiting for you to run something.
It paused partway.
Or it declined.
Your code reads that note, and does something different for each one.
But here's what the note never says.
It never says the job is done.
It only says the model stopped talking.
The technical name for that note is the stop_reason field.
The Messages API, the application programming interface you call directly, documents seven values.
One. end_turn.
Two. max_tokens.
Three. stop_sequence.
Four. tool_use.
Five. pause_turn.
Six. refusal.
And seven. model_context_window_exceeded.
The documentation's advice is blunt.
Always check stop_reason.
Let's take three of them now.
tool_use means the model has asked for one or more tools, and is waiting.
Your loop runs every requested call, then continues.
end_turn means the model finished its turn on its own.
That's your normal exit.
But it is only a candidate for success.
Never proof.
stop_sequence means the model emitted one of the stop strings you configured.
A companion field tells you which one fired, so you branch on that.
The other four, we'll take one at a time.
Quick recap before the first question.
The model always tells you why it stopped.
It never tells you the job is done.
You branch on the reason.
Question one.
The waiter who walks away too early.
Here's the scenario.
An invoice extraction agent runs a hand-written loop.
The loop exits as soon as the first content block of a response is text.
About one invoice in twelve ends with no record, and no error.
The transcripts show a final response with a short line of text.
Something like "let me check the vendor master first".
Followed by a tool request.
What's going on?
Take a second.
Think of a waiter who hears a diner say "hmm, let me think," and walks away.
The words sounded like the end.
But the diner hadn't closed the menu.
They were about to order.
The answer.
In exam terms, one response can carry a text block and a tool_use block together.
The model often thinks out loud before calling a tool, and that's normal.
The stop_reason on that response is tool_use.
The model is waiting for a result.
A loop that checks the type of the first content block exits in the middle of the task.
And it silently drops the tool call.
The fix is to branch on stop_reason.
Continue on tool_use.
And handle every other value explicitly.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: max_tokens is too low, and the response was truncated.
Why?
Truncation shows up as a max_tokens stop reason with incomplete content.
These transcripts contain a complete tool request.
Wrong: the vendor master tool returned an empty result.
Why?
That tool never ran.
The loop exited first.
Wrong: a missing turn cap, and a scheduler killing long runs.
Why?
A scheduler kill leaves no clean final response.
These runs have one.
The constraint that decides it is the phrase "a text block followed by a tool_use block."
Content type and stop_reason measure different things.
Hold on to this line.
Branch on why the model stopped, never on what it happened to say.
Question two.
The pen pal who forgets everything.
Here's the scenario.
To cut token spend, an engineer changes the loop.
After each tool call, it sends back only the tool result.
It skips the assistant message that held the tool request.
Requests start failing with errors on the second iteration.
Why?
Take a second.
Picture a pen pal who forgets everything between letters.
If you reply "yes, here is the answer" without restating their question, they can't make sense of it.
Every letter has to carry the whole thread.
The answer.
The Messages API is stateless.
It keeps nothing between calls.
Your loop owns the history, and must send all of it, every time.
There are three formatting rules.
Break any of them, and you get an API error.
Not a weaker answer.
An error.
First.
You append the assistant message that contains the tool_use block.
Each tool_use block carries an id.
Second.
You follow it immediately with a user message holding one tool_result per tool_use id.
Each result's tool_use_id field matches.
Nothing goes in between.
Third.
Inside that user message, the tool_result blocks come first, before any text.
A tool_result can also carry an optional is_error flag, for reporting a failed call.
So what happens if you remove the assistant message?
The tool_result points at an id that no longer exists.
The request is rejected.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: the API remembers the assistant turn on the server, and a stale session id needs refreshing.
Why?
The Messages API holds no server-side memory at all.
Wrong: the result lacks is_error set to false.
Why?
That flag is optional.
Its absence can't cause a rejection.
Wrong: max_tokens is too low.
Why?
Output length has nothing to do with a malformed history.
And if you want to save tokens?
Trim the tool output instead.
Hold on to this line.
The API forgets everything.
So every request carries the full history, and every tool result sits right after the request it answers.
Now the length limits.
In plain words, a response can be cut off for two different reasons.
Either the answer itself ran out of room.
Or the whole working space was already full.
To careless code, they look the same.
Why?
Because a cut-off answer arrives looking just like a finished one.
Think of a filing cabinet so full that nothing new fits.
Buying a bigger envelope for the report doesn't help.
The problem is the cabinet, not the envelope.
In exam terms, here are the two.
First. max_tokens means the output hit the max_tokens limit you set on the request.
The response is truncated.
The fix is to raise the limit, or continue the response.
Second. model_context_window_exceeded means the response filled the model's entire context window.
That's also truncation.
But raising max_tokens can't help.
The window is full, no matter how large the output allowance is.
So what do you do instead?
You compact the conversation.
Summarise.
Or move the work into subagents that each start with a fresh window.
In both cases, you never parse the truncated output as a finished artifact.
One small detail from the notes. model_context_window_exceeded is typed only in the software development kits' beta namespace.
And on models older than Claude Sonnet four point five, it needs a beta header.
Handle it either way.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A contract extraction pipeline processes merger bundles of several hundred pages, in one conversation.
On the largest bundles, the final response arrives with model_context_window_exceeded.
And the partial JSON is stored as if complete.
The team proposes doubling max_tokens.
What's the right answer?
Take a second.
The answer.
Mark the response truncated.
Then compact the context, or move per-document extraction into fresh subagents.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: double max_tokens.
Why?
That's the remedy for a different stop reason.
Wrong: retry at a lower temperature.
Why?
It doesn't change how much context the bundle consumes.
It's a global remedy, applied without a diagnosis.
And the nastiest trap.
Wrong: a JSON repair step that closes the unterminated brackets.
Why?
That produces valid JSON with missing clauses.
It looks complete downstream.
And that is worse than a visible failure.
The notes add a close cousin.
A nightly batch.
On about two percent of nights, the parser fails on malformed JSON.
And on a few nights, it stores an invoice with three of its eleven line items missing.
Both symptoms are the same thing.
Truncation, passed downstream as if finished.
And they won't reproduce interactively.
Why not?
Because short test documents never hit the limits.
Hold on to this line. max_tokens means the envelope was too small. model_context_window_exceeded means the cabinet is full.
Neither is a finished answer.
Next, pause_turn.
In plain words, sometimes the model is doing a lot of work inside a single turn, and hits an internal step limit.
It stops.
It effectively leaves a note saying it paused here, and someone should pick it up.
It has not finished.
Picture a courier who reaches the end of a shift halfway through a route.
They leave a note: "route paused at stop ten."
If the dispatcher files that note as delivered, half the parcels never arrive.
The technical name is the pause_turn stop reason.
It appears when a server-side tool loop, such as the built-in web search, reaches its iteration limit.
That limit defaults to ten.
It's a continuation point, not a completion.
You append the assistant content to the history, and send another request.
The same turn resumes, without redoing earlier work.
Question four.
Here's the scenario.
A research assistant uses server-side web search.
The loop continues only on tool_use, and returns the text for anything else.
On broad questions, answers stop mid-thought, with no error.
The logs show pause_turn.
Which fix costs least?
Take a second.
The answer.
Append the assistant content, and send another request.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: raise max_tokens.
Why?
Output truncation reports max_tokens, not pause_turn.
Wrong: treat it like a refusal, and retry on a fallback model.
Why?
That throws away progress and doubles cost.
Wrong: raise the loop's own turn cap.
Why?
That cap never fired.
The loop exited because it misread pause_turn as completion.
refusal is the opposite case.
It's terminal for that path.
A companion field called stop_details is filled in only on a refusal.
It names the policy category that triggered it.
For every other stop reason, it's null.
The correct action?
Read stop_details.
Then either retry on a fallback model, or escalate.
You never loop on a refusal.
So when do you use which?
Here's the contrast, one at a time.
tool_use: run the tools, and continue.
end_turn: exit, then check the work yourself.
max_tokens: truncated.
So raise the limit, or continue.
model_context_window_exceeded: truncated.
So shrink what one context holds.
pause_turn: not finished.
So send it back.
refusal: stop this path.
Read stop_details.
Fall back, or escalate.
stop_sequence: read which one fired.
Hold on to this line. pause_turn means still going, send it back. refusal means stop here and escalate.
A quick word on the study material itself, because the sources disagree here.
The lesson one slide deck says end_turn is the only valid exit from a loop.
The written notes go further.
They treat max_tokens and model_context_window_exceeded as truncation exits.
They treat pause_turn as a continuation.
And they add a code-checked acceptance test on top of end_turn.
Do these really conflict?
Not really.
The deck describes the normal, happy exit.
The notes describe everything a production loop must handle.
So on the exam.
If a question asks for the normal completion signal, the answer is end_turn.
If it asks how a loop should handle truncation, a paused server tool, or a claim of success, use the fuller picture from the notes.
Now the heart of this part.
Termination.
In plain words, a loop can fail in four different ways.
One.
It can run too long.
Two.
It can run too expensive.
Three.
It can run stuck.
Busy, but going nowhere.
Four.
It can run wrong.
Stopping, and claiming success, when the work was never done.
No single counter catches all four.
Picture a new hire.
They say "done" at the end of every shift.
And they keep phoning the same supplier, who never answers.
A good manager needs two checks.
First, look for the signed delivery note before accepting "done".
Second, step in when the same call has been made three times with nothing new.
Asking the hire to try harder?
That fixes neither.
The technical version.
You need four independent termination guards.
One.
A turn cap.
It bounds the worst case in round trips.
Two.
A budget cap.
It bounds it in money.
Why do you need both?
Because a single turn that reads a huge file can cost more than twenty cheap turns.
So a turn cap does not bound spend.
Three.
No-progress detection.
It catches the loop that is busy and stuck.
The usual technique is to record a signature for each tool call, meaning the tool name plus its arguments.
Then halt after a bounded run of consecutive turns with no new signature.
The notes use a limit of three.
Four.
An acceptance check.
It's run by your code, rather than claimed by the model.
It decides whether an end_turn is actually a success.
The loop then returns a status the caller must inspect.
Such as complete, halted, truncated, or refused.
Question five.
This one is pick two.
Here's the scenario.
A refund agent has a turn cap of thirty, and exits on end_turn.
Some cases are logged as resolved, with no refund issued and no ticket.
And some runs call lookup_order with identical arguments until the cap fires.
Leadership wants both failure classes caught, without raising cost.
Which two?
Take a second.
The answers.
First.
Have code verify that a refund id or escalation ticket exists before any case is logged as resolved.
Second.
Hash each tool name plus its arguments, and halt after a bounded run of turns with no new call signature.
Each guard catches a failure the other cannot.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: a system prompt sentence telling the agent not to finish until the issue is fully resolved.
Why?
That's advisory.
The model can still end its turn on an unresolved case.
Wrong: raise the cap to sixty.
Why?
It makes the stuck runs more expensive.
And it still doesn't notice nothing is happening.
Wrong: scan the final reply for the word "resolved".
Why?
Parsing the model's own words to decide completion is a named anti-pattern.
Wording varies.
And the word can appear without evidence.
Question six.
A related one from the notes.
Here's the scenario.
An incident agent calls log_search with the identical query fifteen or twenty times.
Each time, it gets the same empty result.
It only stops when an hourly token allowance cuts it off.
The loop already has a turn cap of two hundred.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
No-progress detection.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: lower the cap to forty.
Why?
That just makes the failure cheaper, without detecting it.
Wrong: mark the empty result with is_error.
Why?
It's plausible, and harmful.
An empty result is a valid answer.
Calling it an error invites more retries.
Wrong: set tool_choice to auto.
Why?
It does nothing. auto is already the permissive default.
The words in a stem that point you here.
"Identical calls, repeatedly" points to no-progress detection.
"Resolved without evidence" points to an acceptance check.
Question seven.
One more on termination, and this one is about the cap itself.
Here's the scenario.
A pull request review agent in continuous integration runs a loop while its iteration counter is below six.
When the counter hits six, it posts whatever it has as the finished review.
Small pull requests finish in three iterations.
Large ones get cut off.
And their partial reviews are posted as complete.
What's the right design?
Take a second.
A kitchen timer stops a pot boiling dry.
But a cook who serves every dish the moment the timer rings will serve raw roasts and burnt toast.
The timer is the backstop.
The cook still checks whether the food is done.
The answer.
In exam terms, an iteration cap is a circuit breaker, not a termination condition.
The right design makes stop_reason the primary exit, and keeps the counter as a safety valve.
When the counter fires, the run is reported as halted.
Never as complete.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: raise the counter to thirty.
Why?
It's still the primary stop.
And it still posts partial reviews as complete whenever it fires.
Wrong: remove the counter, and rely only on end_turn.
Why?
That deletes the safety valve, and leaves runaway runs unbounded.
You demote the cap.
You do not delete it.
Wrong: end each review with the phrase "REVIEW COMPLETE", and exit when it appears.
Why?
That's parsing words again.
Hold on to this line.
The model stopping is a candidate.
Your code decides success.
And the cap only bounds the worst case, and reports halted.

Not defensive.
